newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - EBRD says much still to do in eastern Europe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EBRD says much still to do in eastern Europe.

text.p: EBRD chief Jacques de Larosiere on Tuesday pledged the bank's continued support to the former Soviet bloc's most successful economies, saying they still needed help to become Western-style market democracies.

Western countries have begun suggesting that the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), set up in 1991 to aid the transition from communism to free market economies, should scale down operations in countries such as Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Slovenia.
"It is true that there has been somewhat of a pause in those countries," de Larosiere told a news conference at the end of the bank's annual meeting .
But he added that they had not reached the point where the EBRD could pull out.

"I think we are going to see a reactivation of our activities," he said. "We will deepen our impact in the countries at advanced stages of transition, focussing on those areas where we are additional."

De Larosiere said the bank could do a lot in the financial sector, in infrastructure and in environmental work. More involvement was also needed in restructuring companies at various stages of privatisation.
"We will, however, move out of and on from any sector where we cease to be additional," he said.
De Larosiere's words will be welcome particularly to the Poles and Hungarians, who told the bank's annual meeting they were not yet ready to be weaned off bank assistance.

"Even in the most advanced countries in transition, there is still a great demand for the Bank's financing in areas where it can be additional, having significant transition impact and meeting sound banking criteria," Polish National Bank Governor Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.
"Despite our progress in the market transition, the EBRD still has room to expand in Poland," she said.

Some Western bankers argue that states on the threshold of European Union membership no longer need EBRD backing and say the bank should focus on less developed countries further east -- particularly in the former Soviet Union.
De Larosiere said the bank had alredy extended the geographical range of its operations.
But Tibor Draskovics, state secretary at the Hungarian finance ministry, said leading reformers faced tough economic adjustments as they prepared to join the EU and other bodies.
"We will have to implement further tough changes that other countries, which do not aspire to join these institutions, will not have to face in the coming years," he said.

Western countries and top EBRD officials have taken a tougher tone with the former communist countries, warning against any slippage in economic performance and making clear there can no room for complacency on legal reform and the battle against crime and corruption

"If you want to attract capital, people must be relatively comfortable on the way they are going to be treated," de Larosiere said. The bank, founded in a blaze of reformist zeal, has in the past been accused of a lack of financial control.
De Larosiere said 1997 would be the EBRD's fourth year with zero growth in its budget.
But the administrative chaos which marred the opening days of the meeting, when organisers were overwhelmed by the 5,300 delegates who tried to register, was not due to his "stinginess," he said

For personal reasons he was still undecided whether he would accept the second term as bank president which has already been offered. "I'm very attached to this bank and very enthusiastic about it," he said.
